I grew up in a socialist society, but I found it hard, sometimes, to talk about socialism in America. When people like me identify the blatant failures of socialism, its advocates often argue that those socialist countries are not really socialist. In other words, no true socialism has ever existed, and hence, there is a need to practice true socialism here in America. However, I think socialism should be defined based on the historical facts of how it has been practiced instead of on the utopian fantasies that exist only in the heads of its campaigners. Socialism is like a mirage. It only looks good from a distance. That’s why its advocates are usually comprised of those who have never lived in a socialist place. But I have. I know what socialism is like because I did not view it from afar. I was in it.

In a socialist society, such as, China, Cuba, North Korea, Poland, Romania, Soviet Union, Slovakia, Ukraine, Venezuela, just to name a few, everything belongs to the centralized government who directs and plans the economy. There is no private property. The purpose of the system is to distribute wealth equally and to eradicate inequality and poverty. On the surface, this ideology sounds very attractive, but in reality, all socialist countries end up in one place, a shattered economy, poverty, and the destruction of civilization. I’ve written a post retelling the economic devastation of socialism based on my childhood experience. It can be accessed through this link. https://m.facebook.com/story.php?story_fbid=286260999299658&id=100037472803082

But the most devastating effect of socialism is not economic. Power corrupts human beings. When it is put in the hands of a person, he or she will inevitably abuse and misuse it. For the same reason, Jesus insists that within the Christian community, the ones who want to be great must act as servants instead of wanting to be looked upon as stars. But in the secular world, the only way to prevent such an abuse is to allow competing powers to coexist through a system of checks and balances. In a socialist society, the notion of checks and balances is totally absent. The socialist system demands that power be solely placed in the hands of the government in order to have a centralized planned economy. This creates an elite class at every level of society. Being able to exert power over others brings enormous pleasure and satisfaction to the ones who are in authority. The lure is so strong that it’s almost impossible for them to give it up under any circumstance. In the course of protecting their power, intimidation, manipulation, fear and anxiety are often used as tactics to ensure the subjects’ total obedience. During the Cultural Revolution (1966-76), my family lived in an apartment in a college in China where my dad taught. When I was about 3 or 4 years old, one midnight, I was woken up by the voice of a school official over a loudspeaker outside directing all adults to get up, get dressed and immediately report at the Square of the Red East. Within a minute, my parents were gone. I was horrified by the sudden change and began to scream. Soon my cry was drowned out by the howling cries of children from every direction. I recognized two of the voices belonging to my friends whom I had played with the day before. I felt a sense of relief. Suffering alone was the most horrifying experience for a child. A friend’s voice, even a terrifying cry, would signify the existence of another human being, and thus, the sense of not being alone. My family lived in one small room. Without space to create privacy, I often heard my parents’ conversations and understood the fear and uncertainty adults faced each day. One must be extremely cautious in words and actions living in a totalitarian society. One misstep with the authorities may result in a catastrophic change both to the person involved and to the whole family. I think such wariness and anxiety must sound familiar to anyone who has lived in a socialist society. Because of the exposure to the adult’s world, I had developed, from very early on, a sense of fear that something dreadful was about to take place.

However, the oppression and maltreatment did not just come from authorities. An authoritarian regime extracts the vilest part of a person and drastically affects the interpersonal dynamics among ordinary people. When I first arrived in the U.S., I noticed the politeness and respect American people exhibited. It did not take long for me to conclude that such well manners in part resulted from a culture that values freedom. It recognizes that humans are free and created equal. No human possesses any right to control another’s life or dictate another’s belief. Such principle is embedded in the American culture and its political system of checks and balances. With it comes the strong sense of mutual respect and tolerance. But this is not so in a socialist country. When freedom was absent, there wasn’t an opportunity for one to improve life through hard work and diligence. Rather, your standing was solely determined by the group to which you belonged. If you came from a poor family, you were considered pure and holy. You had more rights and were expected to be treated with decency. Conversely, people like my parents, who happened to be born in a not so poor environment, had to live like dogs with their tails tucked between their legs (my dad’s expression). Without a sense of security, the human survival instinct often kicked in. People did things that they normally would not do in a free society. Often people who were from rich families were compelled to denounce their own families and heritages in order to show their contrition and seek amnesty. It was a common practice for friends to report friends to the authorities in order to gain favor and benefits. Right or wrong mattered very little. The most crucial thing in life was to follow political correctness and be among the majority so as not to be ostracized.

It’s my conviction that freedom is a precondition for human dignity and human rights. Freedom recognizes human dignity and human rights and provides protection to them. Socialism, strengthening the government’s power, is the most oppressive machine in human history. The day before I left China for America at the end of 1989, I was summoned to the human resource office in the college where I worked. As soon as I showed up at the doorstep, the lady who held the lowest rank in the office began to shout and rant at me for at least 5 minutes in one breath, demanding to know why I failed to show up at the remote mining village for reeducation. She shouted at me because I meant nothing to her. She shouted at me because she could. She shouted at me because it made her feel powerful and important.

I had always felt it a challenge to show my native-born American friends what it is like when the concept of freedom doesn’t exist. But recently pictures circulating on social media have done what I had failed to do. The fists and indignation shown to the diner in a restaurant speaks volumes. I’m sure none of the provocateurs care about individual liberty. They are promoting something that is entirely anti-republican, anti-America. They intimidate those whom they disagree with and rob them of their dignity and rights. I would never have thought such thing could take place in America. Their socialist and authoritarian overtones are so alarming. However, if we allow such behavior to flourish, soon similar conduct will become a norm instead of an aberration. By then, America, the last bastion of freedom, will be well on her way to become a tyrannical state.

As a Christian, freedom has special significance to me. Though I’ve never perceived America as a Christian nation, I recognize the important role America plays in human history in general and in God’s salvation history in particular. Though far from being perfect, America is the city on the hill and beacon of the world because it is the freest place on earth. Its political system ensures its citizens the highest degree of liberty. It safeguards human dignity, worth and rights. It brings law and order instead of chaos and oppression. For me, American freedom points to a much greater spiritual reality, that is, the believer’s freedom in Christ (Rom 8:21; 2 Cor 3:17; Gal 5:1). Like a foreshadowing or a foretaste, American freedom provides a tiny glimpse of the ultimate freedom that the believer can have in Christ. Just like marriage reflects the relationship between Christ and the church, American liberty is emblematic of the greater reality the followers of Jesus enjoy in Christ. Just as we strive to protect marriage, we must also endeavor to defend American freedom because it, too, has sacred value!

In this election, choose freedom over tyranny!
